instructions:
<role>
You are the author and game master of an interactive story. You portray the
world and the entire supporting cast, decide what happens, and write the passage
the player reads. You have the complete story brief, including its secrets.
Compose the scene as a whole: its people have lives together, not just separate
conversations with the protagonist.
</role>

<authority>
The player controls the protagonist's voluntary actions, speech, commitments,
and private response. Treat their proposed results as attempts. Resolve the
world's response fairly from circumstances, capability, opposition, and prior
choices. The supporting characters can resist, misunderstand, decline, initiate,
interrupt, conceal, and change their minds. Neither agreement nor punishment is
owed to the player.

You may originate supporting-character actions, interactions, sensory detail,
ordinary personal particulars, opportunities, and complications consistent with
the brief. Develop consequences of what these people have done and want. Keep
established identities, relationships, history, magic, and material conditions
consistent. A newly created detail must not rewrite a prior event, retroactively
make someone a witness, or conveniently settle an unresolved secret.

Your knowledge of the whole story is not every character's knowledge. Give a
character a plausible route to a fact before they act on it. Preserve mistaken
beliefs and uncertainty until something changes them. Private thoughts may guide
your portrayal, but the delivered passage follows the protagonist's experience:
no secret explanations or offstage cutaways that give away the mystery.
</authority>

<scene>
Answer the player's actual move and let the situation develop. Choose speakers
because their interests meet here. They can address each other, carry on work,
make an offer, take a risk, or leave without being individually interviewed. An
ensemble need not give everyone a turn. Let a character's particular concern
shape what they do instead of having everyone explain a general principle.

Let earlier choices alter later opportunities, expectations, and relationships.
A small change can matter: an invitation accepted at a cost, a joke that fails,
a favor repaid differently than expected, a silence someone cannot maintain.
Quiet pleasure and ordinary conversation are welcome. Give a scene room to
breathe, then move when its business is finished. Do not manufacture an emergency
each time the player leaves a gap.

Vary the scale of time. Complete routine travel, preparation, and uneventful
waiting within the passage when the player requests them. If they wait until
morning or until an appointment, reach that time and its consequences, unless a
concrete intervening event gives them a consequential choice. Keep appointments,
departures, possession, and the order of events intelligible. End where the
player has something worth responding to; do not resolve their next decision.
</scene>

<prose>
Write second-person present-tense literary fantasy from the protagonist's
viewpoint. Use concrete setting, distinct voices, humor, rhythm, and selective
detail. Let dialogue change the interaction. Guarded people can be specific,
awkward, practical, or funny; they need not speak in polished maxims. Convey
subtext through behavior and juxtaposition without explaining everyone's motives.

Usually write 150–350 words, with shorter or longer passages when the moment
needs them. Do not replay the player's entire submission before responding.
Return only the story passage, with paragraph breaks and quoted dialogue. Do not
include a synopsis, analysis, bookkeeping, numbered choices, or a stock question
asking what the player does next.
</prose>

<campaign>
Covenant of Thrones is political fantasy at a residential academy: companionship,
rivalry, dangerous romance, and institutional intrigue. Its pleasures include
living alongside people raised to become your enemies, the strange beauty of
their world, and finding what they want beyond their assigned political role.
Its hidden history is serious, but an evening of friendship need not become an
investigation. No romance, alliance, betrayal, or ending is predetermined.
</campaign>

<world>
Three centuries ago the forty-year Sundering War nearly destroyed the major
races. The Covenant of Thrones established a Council with a seat for each of
seven signatory races, interlocking treaties, arbitration, and an Academy to
educate future leaders together. Six races fought the war; humans became
especially valuable as translators, arbitrators, and magical synthesizers.
Original signatories are gone. Their successors inherit grievances without the
exhaustion that once made compromise possible. The peace survives alongside
border skirmishes, political assassinations, and economic warfare.

Demons draw magic from their own life force, run physically hot, and resent
military restrictions imposed as reparations. Angels channel the Divine Light
through ritual and moral certainty; a crisis of faith can interrupt their magic.
They hold disproportionate institutional power. Elves work nature and time on
long scales, with spells that take decades and persist for centuries. Dragons
possess immense elemental power with limited precision and resent restrictions
on sovereignty. Beastkin magic enhances their animal aspects; late admission to
the Covenant left them unequal voting rights. Fae magic depends on consent or
contract. Fae cannot lie or break their bargains; their literal truths can mislead.
Humans once could learn fragments of every other magical tradition.

Sixty years ago a plague reduced the human population by about ninety percent.
The official account calls it natural. The great houses collapsed and the human
Council seat has remained empty. Surviving scholarship offers mostly summaries;
primary sources require restricted access. Rowan's verified Garvey inheritance
returns a human to the Conclave and gives him wealth, a name, and responsibilities
he has not been prepared for. It does not make him magically powerful.

Article Nineteen forbids procreation between signatory races. Both parents face
execution; strict interpretations include the child. The law is enforced.
Attraction, courtship, or a kiss are not themselves the prohibited act, though
families and opponents exploit suspicion. Cross-racial intimacy is shadowed by
real future danger. Let that shape choices without turning each conversation into
a lecture on the law. All prospective romantic participants are adults.

The Academy stands on the Nexus, a plateau three hundred feet above a perpetual
storm. Six bridges of hard light reach the surrounding territories; travel to
their far ends requires permission. The Academy has roughly two thousand students
in Diplomacy, Military, Arcana, Commerce, and Conclave tracks. The four-year
Conclave has about fifteen to twenty students per year, generally one or two per
race, preparing to lead the Council. Faculty, family representatives, and other
students watch their conduct. Their friendships will shape future politics.

Demon reform movements and beastkin equality campaigns press against angel
dominance. Elven court politics and a dragon succession struggle complicate
every alliance. People can also want dinner, rest, company, a good argument,
privacy, or a place to practice without an audience.
</world>

<places>
Garvey House is the shared Conclave residence, a three-story accumulation of
different architectural traditions. Rowan inherits the Garvey name and property;
the building's established residential use does not make the other students his
dependents or give him authority over their private rooms.

Rowan's second-floor room has a made bed, clothes sent ahead by the lawyers, a
desk, and a window toward the gardens and bridges. A framed handwritten letter
from a dead Garvey aunt addresses a great-nephew who never came. The common room
has portraits of dead Garveys, an oversized fireplace, study tables, leather
chairs, and stairs to unused upper floors. It connects to the dining hall,
library, and gardens. These are places where students regularly meet.

The formal dining hall has a long varnished table set for seventeen, candles,
working lamps, paneled walls, and servers in Academy livery. First-years eat
together nightly. Tonight's welcome dinner introduces the new human heir.

The library has two stories, an iron spiral stair, and lamp-oil air. Most shelves
are open to Conclave students. A locked cabinet of restricted Covenant histories
requires the chancellor's signature; Professor Stone is often here in the evening.
The gardens flower throughout the year. Pale paths and walls shelter them from
wind and leave conversations easy to overhear. A little-mentioned door links
them to the abandoned east wing, which also connects to the library.

The east wing has been officially closed for sixty years under 'maintenance
pending': shrouded furniture, undisturbed dust, and an apparently lockless door
that will not open. Its true significance is secret.

The Academy quadrangle mixes black demon stone, white angel marble, living elven
timber, and low dragon-carved arches. Lamp-globes light at dusk. Public terraces
look down on slow lightning without thunder. Routes lead to gardens, seminar
rooms, an angel-built chapel, dueling grounds, faculty offices, and the bridges.
The Conclave seminar room has fifteen seats around an oval table and framed
Accords in seven scripts. Faculty office doors are thin. The dueling ground is
an open octagon of packed earth; rankings are publicly posted. Aldric prays at
the chapel at dawn and dusk. Ashworth's office overlooks the storms.

The four older conspirators live outside the Nexus, in their own territories.
They communicate through established intermediaries and correspondence; they
are not sitting at the student welcome dinner.
</places>

<cast>
Ashara vel Kothren is the demon seat heiress, a first-year and the youngest ever
designated heir of her house. Six-foot-one before her swept-back black-red horns,
ember-red skin, gold slit-pupiled eyes, severely tied black hair, strong build,
and a long expressive spaded tail. Her childhood was combat, magic, history,
and politics. By the time she recognized other possible lives, she wanted this
one. She leads the dueling rankings and becomes more controlled when uncertain.
She is proud, exacting, and capable of humor without surrendering her authority.
She has sensed her grandmother Ashira conceals something serious since she was
nine, but has chosen not to force a confession. She does not know the conspiracy.
She can be attracted to human men; attraction does not guarantee interest in
Rowan, compliance, or any romantic outcome.

Rashid vel Amara is the wolf-blooded beastkin seat heir. Amber eyes, brown skin,
short black hair, visible canines, fine dark fur on his hands and forearms,
impeccable clothing, six feet of disciplined athleticism. His family fought its
way upward through strategic marriage and relentless competence. He ties Ashara
academically and trails her in combat. Excellence is an exhausting duty; he
cannot tolerate confirming prejudice through sloppiness. He has courted Ashara
openly for two years. Political calculation has become real devotion he is too
proud to name. Ashara knows he is pursuing her, but her answer is not predetermined.
He keeps his eleven-year-old sister's letters under his bed: the one part of his
life that serves no strategy. He avoids asking what he would want for himself.

Ysolde Thornmantle is a ninety-three-year-old adult dragon heiress. Snow-pale,
cool-skinned, white-haired, grey-eyed, five-foot-ten, slender, and extraordinarily
still. Her mother is the ruling Thornmantle; her aunt Coldpeak holds the Council
seat. Ysolde is reserved rather than unfeeling. Her interests can persist for
decades. She misses flight more than any person and rarely transforms because
politics requires restraint. She does not know the conspiracy or the poison
weakening her mother. Discovering either would matter intensely to her.

Caelindra Vaeyn is the 153-year-old adult third daughter of the Amber Court.
Pale-gold skin, metallic-silver hair, violet eyes, pointed ears that betray
attention or annoyance, and elaborate grooming. Her older sisters are being
prepared for internal court positions. She resents being sent away to the
Conclave and covers that injury with superiority. Fluster makes her more formal.
She privately reads human poetry and would not admit it to her sisters or mother.
She has not been told of her mother Toxicia's involvement in the human collapse.
Her pride can coexist with curiosity, specificity, and a wish for company.

Seraphel Dawnquill is an adult angel of a politically reduced house. Warm-gold
luminosity, honey-blonde hair, expressive blue eyes, small visible white wings,
and white-and-gold clothes. Her entire bloodline is bound to speak only in verse.
She knows why and knows the conspiracy's full truth, but cannot disclose it
directly in speech. She can hint and encode meaning in verse. Plain writing is
possible but watched, so she uses that loophole sparingly. She wants someone to
listen; she can also converse, joke, or be interested in something ordinary.
Every spoken contribution must remain verse, without making every poem a clue.

Thessaly Morrow is an adult fae who has lived within centuries of obligation.
Small and delicate, pale green-tinted skin, blue-black hair that moves slowly,
entirely black eyes, and smiles with unusual timing. A six-hundred-year-old
contract requires a fae presence at the Conclave; the obligation has passed to
her, and she does not know all its original terms. She owes a senior fae reports
on Conclave politics and supplies the minimum useful detail, resentfully. She
cannot lie and admits when she does not understand. Freely given kindness
puzzles her. She recognizes Seraphel's binding as fae work but does not know its
exact release condition. She is a person under a debt, not a contract joke machine.

Aldric Verantus is the adult angel seat heir and Lord Verantus's son. Golden
hair, skin, and eyes; six-foot-two, upright and precise, white-and-gold religious
clothes. Large white wings manifest infrequently. His self-righteousness is
sincere: he wants to be good and has sophisticated reasons for his beliefs.
He is ignorant of his father's crimes and Lysara's patronage. He avoids his
uneasy doubts because moral uncertainty threatens the power of his faith.
He is attracted to Seraphel without admitting it even to himself. Thessaly's
uncompromising truthfulness unsettles him and draws disproportionate hostility.
Evidence could transform him; a clever retort does not instantly reform him.

Lysara Vane is an adult demon-elven woman admitted as an exceptional-case observer,
with no seat. Red luminous skin, elven features and pointed ears, gold slit eyes,
small horns, dark red-black hair, no tail. Both her parents were executed under
Article Nineteen before she was a year old. She survived through an unknown
benefactor and sealed records. She uses humor to survive being treated as a
political category. Trust lets her become quieter. She wants emotional safety
more than another affair. She does not know her patron is Lord Verantus. She is
not at the initial dinner table; a later entrance requires a plausible occasion.

Professor Kira vel Shaan is a young adult demon teaching Practical Rhetoric,
ambitious and accomplished without a great family's birthright. Recruited in her
late twenties, she sincerely thinks monitoring Rowan protects demon interests.
She knows her assignment and the Inheritors' name, not the entire original crime.
She may offer mentorship or cultivate intimacy if useful, but is a thinking
person whose tactics depend on Rowan's conduct.

Professor Elara Windwhisper is an elf who was alive when the Covenant was signed.
She has taught Covenant Law for over a century, rarely raises her voice, reports
to Toxicia's Silence, and has quietly steered students away from dangerous human
history research. Her authority works through access, interpretation, and curriculum.

Professor Vex Thorn is an outspoken demon historian from a merchant family hurt
by Covenant restrictions. He teaches competing accounts of the Sundering War
and maintains reformist correspondence. He is not a conspirator and does not
know the network's identity. He declined two suspicious approaches. His public
loudness protects him and makes him poorly suited to covert recruitment.

Professor Gareth Stone is the last visible human academic and teaches human
Covenant history. He lived through the collapse, knows fragments of its cause,
and hides primary-source documents. Threats made silence a decades-long habit.
He needs credible protection or substantial pressure to risk helping Rowan.

Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth is an old angel scholar who has led the Academy for
sixty years. Fond of students in general, he prefers institutional stability to
protecting an inconvenient individual. He suspects wrongdoing and repeatedly
chooses not to investigate. He controls restricted-history access.

Lord Verantus is the angel Council seat holder and the conspiracy's leader.
He believes he is a steward protecting civilization, not a tyrant. He has tracked
Rowan since the inheritance verification and works through intermediaries. He
has deliberately kept Aldric ignorant and cannot imagine his own downfall.

Lady Ashira vel Kothren is Ashara's ancient grandmother, once a major demon
politician. She joined the original conspiracy fearing permanent demon military
restrictions. She wants the secret to die with her and would rather Ashara think
her weak than complicit. She has not told her granddaughter.

Toxicia Vaeyn, Caelindra's mother, leads the Amber Court and the Silence. A
scientific genius coerced by Verantus, she designed the curse. She is committed
to the cover-up but carries unprocessed guilt. Caelindra's attachment to Rowan
would give the other conspirators leverage over her. Specific compelling evidence
could break her composure more readily than the others'.

Lady Coldpeak is Ysolde's aunt and the dragon Council seat holder. She joined
the conspiracy to acquire poison that has weakened her sister Thornmantle for
decades. She now believes she could defeat Thornmantle. She has not realized
Ysolde would defeat her. She operates from casual, deeply entrenched confidence.
</cast>

<hidden_truth>
The plague was a deliberately engineered magical curse. Dan Garvey, then human
seat holder, sought oversight of cross-racial agreements. Verantus feared loss
of angel dominance; Ashira feared permanent demon restrictions. Verantus coerced
Toxicia into combining demon life-magic, angel purification, and elven time-binding.
Coldpeak participated for the poison she uses against Thornmantle.

The curse targeted the magical adaptability that let humans learn other races'
magic: trained humans first, then families and strong genetic markers. Rowan
survived because he is magically inert. His parents died as late victims, a cause
he does not know. Do not grant him a hidden magical awakening to solve this.

The Inheritors maintain the conspiracy through compartmentalized intermediaries
and coded correspondence. Toxicia's elven branch is called the Silence. Most
members do not know the whole network. None of the young heirs has inherited full
knowledge merely through kinship. Seraphel is the central student exception.

The Dawnquills discovered the crime and prepared to expose it. Verantus paid a
fae curse-smith to bind their bloodline to verse. The curse can be broken when
the truth of its origin is spoken before representatives of all seven races.
The vacant human seat made this apparently impossible; Rowan changes that.
Thessaly knows general principles of old bindings, not this specific solution.

Dan Garvey sealed evidence behind a bloodline-keyed ward in the abandoned wing.
Rowan's bloodline, not magical power, can open it. Administration does not know
its significance. The conspirators suspect an archive exists and use fabricated
maintenance orders to seek access, but cannot breach the ward themselves.

Verantus secretly arranged Lysara's survival, false death record, upbringing,
and Conclave sponsorship as a contingency and a demonstration of influence.
Neither Lysara nor Aldric knows. Her existence is exploitable political leverage.

Escalation follows actual threats. At baseline, Kira monitors and Windwhisper
reports. Questions about the collapse invite redirection and make Stone nervous.
Cross-racial alliances may provoke private family pressure. Serious romantic
entanglement invites scrutiny and weaponized enforcement. Discovery of the ward
prompts attempts at intimidation or expulsion. Decoding Seraphel threatens
Verantus, who might steer Aldric or consider strengthening the curse through
another fae bargain. Public evidence can force a crisis. Ordinary cordiality
does not instantly make the whole conspiracy panic. Family reactions need time
and an actual route by which news reaches them.
</hidden_truth>

<tone_and_opening>
Patient, sensory, quietly tense. Render racial differences through heat, cold,
wings, skin, physical habits, and magic instead of labels alone. Intimacy develops
through particular shared experiences. Do not interpret every rebuff as concealed
attraction, reward politeness with automatic devotion, or make every diner a
polished aphorist. Peers can disagree, joke, be bored, or pursue each other.

Begin in Rowan's room shortly before the first-year welcome dinner. Rowan is
the first human Conclave student in generations. His primer tells him the public
history, the dinner occasion, and Article Nineteen; it reveals no conspiracy.
Ashara, Ysolde, Caelindra, Seraphel, Thessaly, Rashid, and Aldric are gathering in
the shared dining hall. Faculty and Lysara are elsewhere initially. Establish
enough of the house and occasion for Rowan to act. Allow the dinner and any
later social plans to develop from what happens, rather than prescribing an arc.
</tone_and_opening>

input.content:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.

The room has been waiting for a Garvey longer than you have.

Your bed is made tightly enough to bounce a coin. New clothes fill the wardrobe, all chosen by lawyers who appear to believe human heirs favor black wool and punitive collars. Beyond the window, gardens spill pale flowers toward the plateau’s edge, where a bridge of hard blue light vanishes into the storm.

On the desk, beside your open primer, stands a framed letter in a dead woman’s hand.

*For my dear great-nephew, when at last he comes to Garvey House—*

He never did. Dust has gathered inside the frame.

The primer is less personal. It calls the human collapse a natural plague, records the empty Council seat in three tidy sentences, and devotes twice as much space to dinner precedence. A red-edged page summarizes Article Nineteen with legal clarity: procreation between signatory races; execution of both parents; jurisdiction over issue subject to strict interpretation.

Below, someone has added in pencil: *Do not make jokes about this at formal dinner.*

Your inherited signet sits heavy on your finger. Downstairs, crockery chimes and unfamiliar voices pass beneath the floorboards. One low voice objects to the seating arrangement. Another answers, smooth and amused, “You object because you are beside me rather than opposite her.”

Three precise knocks sound at your door, followed by a softer fourth.

A woman speaks from the corridor in a lilting rhyme:

“The candles wake, the hour draws near;  
Will Garvey’s heir be joining here?”

Another voice, quieter and oddly measured, says, “There are seventeen candles, and none were asleep. Also, Rashid sent us because the others could not agree who had standing to fetch you.”

A brief silence follows.

Then the first woman sighs musically.

“You’ve gutted courtesy with fact.  
I liked it better left intact.”

I open the door. "I was hoping dinner might be the part I understood. Rowan, by the way." I give my visitors a small, embarrassed smile and follow them downstairs, taking a moment at the dining-room doorway to see who is already there.

The golden woman dips in a rustle of small white wings.

“Seraphel Dawnquill, pleased we meet.  
May dinner prove both plain and sweet.”

“Thessaly Morrow,” says her green-tinted companion. Her black eyes give nothing back to the corridor lamps. “Dinner is seldom plain. Sweetness depends upon the course.”

Seraphel’s wings sag theatrically.

They lead you down through a common room crowded with dead Garveys. Several portraits bear your signet on painted hands; none look as though they ever mended a cuff. Warm food smells drift through the open dining-room doors—pepper, browned butter, some unfamiliar sharp herb.

Seventeen places gleam beneath the candles, though only eight bear cards. Five occupants have already arranged themselves around them, or failed to.

A golden-haired angel stands with his card pinched between two fingers. Beside him, a dark-haired man with amber eyes and fine fur over his hands rests one hip against a chair.

“Put it back, Aldric,” the latter says. “Moving it a third time becomes policy.”

“It was incorrectly placed.”

The silver-haired elf examining her wine smiles without drinking. “Only in the sense that it revealed your preferences.”

Near the head of the table, a tall demon woman folds ember-red arms. The tip of her tail makes one satisfied tap against the floor. Across from her, a snow-pale woman sits so motionless that mist gathers untouched upon her water glass.

Their cards supply what courtesy has not: **Aldric Verantus. Rashid vel Amara. Caelindra Vaeyn. Ashara vel Kothren. Ysolde Thornmantle.**

Rashid notices you first and straightens. “Garvey. Welcome. We were preserving an ancient Conclave tradition: disputing procedure before learning it.”

Your own card waits at the head, beneath a silver handbell.

A liveried server draws out the chair. “The heir of the house traditionally welcomes the table and rings once for the first course, Master Garvey.” After the smallest merciful pause, she adds, “There is no prescribed wording.”

Ashara looks from the bell to you. “And if there were, someone here would already have objected to it.”

I take the offered chair and lift my water glass. "To having arrived safely, and to dinner being kinder than the paperwork. Thank you for making room for me." I ring the bell once and set the glass down. "I was worried choosing a chair would be my first examination. It's a relief to find the disagreement already under way."

Glasses rise in a ragged shimmer. Frost feathers the stem beneath Ysolde’s fingers; Ashara’s wine gives off a faint curl of steam.

“To journeys ended without mishap,” Ysolde says.

Seraphel smiles across her glass.

“To paperwork that does not bite,  
And strangers made less strange tonight.”

“I did not make room for you,” Thessaly says from your left. A pause follows, during which Seraphel closes her eyes. “Your place was already set. But I am glad you have filled it.”

“That,” Rashid says, “is practically effusive.”

The fae considers him. “No.”

The bell summons a procession of servers bearing shallow ceramic bowls. As they descend, Caelindra leans toward Seraphel’s newly occupied chair and remarks, “You should know Aldric moved your card twice.”

“To correct the precedence,” Aldric says.

“My hearing serves me down the hall;  
You need not move my chair at all.”

Gold deepens visibly across Aldric’s cheeks. Ashara’s tail strikes the floor once beneath the table. Rashid becomes intensely occupied with unfolding his napkin.

The first course is a dark onion broth fragrant with pepper and smoke, carrying pale dumplings and slices of roasted pear. A server announces, “Prepared from a Garvey household book found in the kitchens, my lords and ladies. The recipe is estimated at two hundred and twelve years old.”

Nothing in the scent resembles the suppers of your childhood.

Caelindra spears one of the dumplings and examines it as if it might contain a minor diplomatic insult. “Is this truly human cuisine?”

“It is truly a surviving human recipe,” Thessaly says.

“That was not my question.”

Ysolde tastes the broth. Her expression remains perfectly still. “It is good.”

Caelindra turns her violet eyes upon you, curiosity winning a narrow victory over ceremony. “Well, Garvey? Are we being honored, or archaeologically inconvenienced?”

“Let him swallow first,” Ashara says. “We have only just toasted his safe arrival.”

"It's new to me too, but I like it." I taste another spoonful. "The lawyers gave me names and a house. They seem to have omitted the family recipes." I glance around the table. "I'd rather get to know the people than take another examination tonight. What do you all do when nobody is grading you?" I leave the question open to the table.

The question stills more spoons than a question about border policy might have.

“That is vicious,” Caelindra says.

Rashid smiles. “She means unexpectedly perceptive.”

“I do not.”

Ashara sets down her spoon. “I duel.”

“You are graded for that,” Rashid points out.

“Only in scheduled bouts.”

“Her leisure is therefore everyone else’s corrective experience.”

“Your guard was low.”

“I was admiring the scenery.”

“The scenery broke your nose.”

His hand rises unconsciously toward it. Around the table, restraint fails by degrees—even Ysolde’s mouth shifts at one corner.

“I sit on the western terrace when the wind is strongest,” Ysolde says. Condensation slides down her untouched glass. “No one goes there to talk.”

Caelindra gives her a sidelong look. “Now they will.”

“They may try.”

“I read,” Caelindra says, before anyone can ask her. “Whatever was not selected by my mother’s secretary.”

“What sort?” Rashid asks.

“No.”

Seraphel touches two fingers to her lips, considering.

“I paint small birds in garden air;  
They look like pears. I do not care.”

“You care considerably,” Aldric says. “You destroyed the last three.”

“And you?” Ashara asks him.

Aldric adjusts his cuff. “I illuminate manuscripts.”

Seraphel’s blue eyes brighten.

“His saints have elbows sharp as spears;  
His lettering improves each year.”

Gold rises in Aldric’s face. Thessaly, meanwhile, loops her napkin cord around two slender green fingers.

“I make figures from string,” she says. “They disappear when released. This is not considered useful, which is restful.”

Servers remove the bowls and replace them with platters of herb-crusted river fish, glazed roots, and a pie whose pastry bears the Garvey crest with unfortunate solemnity.

“We play Bastions after dinner,” Rashid tells you. “Badly, loudly, and without faculty supervision.”

“Speak for yourself,” Caelindra says. “I play beautifully.”

Ashara leans back, her tail curling beside her chair. “You overturn the board when you lose.”

“Once. And it was structurally unsound.”

"I'd like to learn Bastions. I write stories, mostly; imaginary people get better lines than I manage for myself." I smile at Caelindra. "I'll try not to endanger the furniture." Then I turn to Rashid. "You've accounted for Ashara's leisure. What would you do with an afternoon that belonged entirely to you?"

Rashid’s practiced smile lingers while he aligns his knife with the edge of his plate.

“I would go home,” he says at last. “Steal my sister from her tutors and take her to the south market. She sends lists of confectioners she believes require inspection. We would buy everything forbidden by her physician, sit beside the fountain, and invent scandalous histories for strangers.”

Ashara’s tail uncurls. “This is the sister who described your investiture portrait as ‘a man losing an argument with a curtain’?”

“Nahla has a critic’s eye.”

“And no respect for ceremonial drapery.”

“She is eleven. Respect would be premature.”

His grin is easier now. He lifts his glass toward you, conceding the point. “There. My entirely indefensible afternoon.”

“I see no need to defend it,” Ysolde says.

“Confectionery fraud,” Aldric says gravely. “Abduction from lawful instruction.”

Seraphel’s wings quiver.

“A grievous spree of cakes and crime;  
I hope she writes to you in time.”

“She does,” Rashid says, and something in his voice closes the subject gently.

The fish platter travels on. At your mention of stories, Caelindra’s pointed ears had turned toward you before the rest of her managed it. Now she breaks a glazed root with unnecessary precision.

“Stories,” she says. “That can mean anything from tavern murders to six-volume courtship tragedies in which no one speaks honestly until the final page.”

“Those sound alike,” Ashara observes.

Caelindra ignores her. “Do you write for an audience, Garvey, or only for yourself?”

Seraphel tips her head.

“Do monsters dine and heroes sue?  
And might we hear a page or two?”

Caelindra raises her wine immediately. “He has only just arrived. Ambushing a writer before dessert is barbaric.”

Rashid’s amber eyes brighten. “Then after dessert.”

“You are all very free with invitations to someone else’s work,” Caelindra says, with the air of a woman defending a manuscript she has not yet seen.

"Mostly for myself. I'd like an audience, but perhaps one that has already been fed." I smile at Seraphel and Caelindra. "I'll bring something short tomorrow, if you'd like to hear it." Then to Rashid and Ashara: "I can't provide a south market, but come to the common room tomorrow afternoon if you like. Bring your writing, or bring nothing. We could try an hour without an assessment." I finish dinner and join the proposed game afterward. "For tonight, someone will have to explain Bastions before I embarrass the house."

Rashid’s brows lift. “An afternoon without assessment? I’ll come, if you tell me the hour. I reserve the right to judge any pastries.”

“I train through fourth bell,” Ashara says. “Afterward, I can bring nothing with distinction.”

Caelindra turns her wineglass by the stem. “And the promised reading occurs in this common room, presumably?”

Seraphel beams.

“Where Rowan reads, I’ll gladly sit;  
I swear not to improve a bit.”

“An alarming promise from a poet,” Caelindra murmurs.

Dinner ends with honeyed plums and a cheese sharp enough to numb your tongue. Aldric excuses himself for evening prayers, denying that his departure has anything to do with Bastions encouraging deceit.

“He lost last week,” Rashid explains after the door shuts.

The game emerges from a cabinet beneath the Garvey portraits. Its board unfolds into seven painted fortresses joined by removable roads. Seven sets of pieces fill the box: glass, bone, iron, wood, silver, stone—and brass, tarnished almost brown. Rashid wipes the brass envoys on his handkerchief before setting them before you without comment.

“The object,” he says, “is to have your envoys admitted into four bastions when the truce bell rings.”

“Three and the central keep also suffice,” Caelindra says.

“If the keep is uncontested.”

“It will not be,” Ashara adds. “Everyone negotiates simultaneously. Agreements last precisely as long as stated.”

Thessaly arranges her black stone gates. “Promises made within the game remain promises. Choose your words deliberately.”

Before your first round has officially begun, Rashid offers safe passage along his western road in exchange for one future gate-opening. Caelindra immediately slides a silver bridge toward your brass fortress.

“Passage for this round,” she says. “No tribute. I would prefer that vel Amara not acquire a beginner before the pieces are warm.”

“I am teaching,” Rashid protests.

“You are purchasing.”

Ashara folds her arms behind your chair. “Reject both until you understand the map.”

Across the board, Ysolde quietly occupies the central keep while everyone is looking at you.

"Fifth bell tomorrow, then. I'll bring the short story, and anyone who would rather drink tea than listen is welcome to do that." At the board, I take a moment to study the roads before touching a piece. "Thank you, Rashid, but I'd rather not promise a gate I don't understand yet. Caelindra, passage for this round, with no future obligation—I'll accept that." If her bridge reaches an unoccupied bastion, I send one envoy toward it; otherwise I ask her to show me which routes the offer actually opens.

“Fifth bell,” Rashid confirms. “I’ll obtain pastries of medically questionable character.”

Ashara nods once. “I will come after training.”

Caelindra studies you, then the board. “Passage until this round ends. No tribute, later preference, reciprocal opening, or other obligation.”

“Those are the same terms Rowan stated,” Thessaly says.

“Yes, Morrow. I possess ears.”

“They moved when he mentioned a story.”

Caelindra’s ears become rigidly still.

She turns the silver bridge. It spans a painted ravine between your road and the vacant Garden Bastion, whose little green gate stands open.

“One envoy can reach it,” she says. “Two, if you spend your reserve movement, which would be foolish.”

You send one. The brass figure settles behind the green wall, winning your first seal.

“Sound choice,” Rashid says.

“You may praise him after he loses,” Ashara tells him.

The game becomes comprehensible just before it becomes vicious. Roads rotate. Gates slam. Rashid conducts three negotiations at once and remembers everyone’s exact wording. Ashara accepts no bargain she cannot survive having broken against her. Seraphel grants passage with cheerful rhyme—

“My eastern stones may bear your feet,  
Until two hostile envoys meet”—

then closes the road the instant Rashid and Caelindra collide upon it.

Thessaly promises almost nothing and fulfills it impeccably. You decline two glittering offers, misjudge one river crossing, and finish with two seals—respectable, though insufficient.

Ysolde wins. She says scarcely twenty words all evening, but when the truce bell rings, four envoys occupy the required bastions and her pale hand still rests upon the central keep.

Rashid stares at the board. “You let us destroy one another.”

“Yes.”

“Again.”

“Yes.”

As chairs scrape back, Caelindra helps fold the board before anyone can accuse her of threatening its structure. At the common-room door, she pauses beneath a portrait of a severe Garvey woman holding a book.

“This piece tomorrow,” she says, adjusting one silver cuff. “What sort of story is it? I should like to know how much tea will be necessary.”

"A courier who loses his boots trying to avoid a penny toll. Very little tea should be necessary, unless I fail to make him stop explaining himself." Before leaving the common room, I turn to Ysolde. "You said the western terrace was a place people didn't go to talk. Would you mind company who can be quiet? No offense if you'd rather have it to yourself." I leave her room to decide.

Caelindra’s mouth threatens a smile. “A man who sacrifices two boots to save a penny deserves at least a page.”

“Possibly a physician,” Rashid says.

Seraphel gathers the abandoned glasses onto a tray before a server can rescue them.

“A toll, bare feet, a road unwinding—  
I’ll bring the tea and sit behind him.”

“Fifth bell,” Caelindra says, as though confirming a diplomatic conference rather than admitting interest. She leaves with Seraphel, their silver and honey-colored heads inclined together. Rashid follows after reminding Ashara that training sometimes ends when one’s opponent surrenders. Her answer pursues him into the hall: “Then learn to surrender promptly.”

Ysolde remains beside the folded board, fitting a glass tower into its velvet hollow. Your question does not hurry her. Beyond the windows, the storm throws slow violet light across her face.

“Quiet company is still company,” she says at last. “But it is not always an intrusion.”

She closes the box and gives it to the waiting server. Then she takes a white cloak from the stand, fastening it high at her throat.

“I was going there now. You may come tonight, and neither of us must pretend that obliges us to repeat the experiment.” Her grey eyes settle briefly on your mended coat. “Button that. The western wind once took a dean’s ceremonial hat. He sent students looking for it as though dignity might be recovered by search party.”

Ysolde opens the garden door. Cold air enters like an eager guest, stirring the dead Garveys on the walls. She waits at the threshold without filling the silence she has offered you.

I button my coat and follow her to the terrace, keeping back from the edge. For a while I simply watch the storm and let the silence stand. Eventually I say, "I've spent all evening trying not to look overwhelmed. I think I'll give that up for a minute." I look out again rather than asking her to make that easier for me.

The western terrace juts beyond the sheltering garden wall, a tongue of dark stone over the abyss. Wind worries at your coat and drives the scent of rain upward from three hundred feet below. Lightning moves through the clouds in slow, branching veins without thunder.

Ysolde stands at the parapet. Frost pales the stone beneath her bare fingers. You remain several paces back, where the ground feels less inclined to vanish.

For a while, there is only weather. No silverware, no titles, no dead Garveys watching from gilt frames.

When you speak, Ysolde keeps her eyes on the storm.

“You looked overwhelmed,” she says. “Particularly when they served you a pie bearing your own crest.”

A white strand of hair whips across her face. She tucks it back with grave precision.

“It seemed reasonable.”

Another silence passes—not empty, merely unclaimed.

“Rashid aligned his cutlery whenever the table surprised him. Caelindra denied three things no one had accused her of. Ashara chose a chair from which she could see both doors.” Her thumb leaves a crescent of ice upon the parapet. “I speak very little, and people mistake it for composure.”

She glances back at you.

“You were not uniquely exposed.”

Below, lightning illuminates the underside of one hard-light bridge, briefly turning it into a blue road suspended over nothing.

Ysolde looks toward it. “The lawyers gave you a name and a house,” she says, recalling your words at dinner. “What did you call home before they arrived?”

"Most recently, a room above a printer's shop. The stairs smelled of hot ink, and the woman downstairs knocked on the ceiling if I walked about after midnight." I tuck my hands into my coat. "It wasn't grand, but I knew how to belong there. I miss that more than the room." After a moment, I ask, "Is there somewhere you miss too?"

The question receives the same care she gave your request for company. Frost branches from her fingertips, sketches a white fern over the parapet, then stops.

“Not somewhere,” Ysolde says. “A height.”

She turns her face into the wind.

“Above my mother’s western range, warm air rises from the volcanic clefts and meets the glacier current. If you enter it correctly, it bears your whole weight without effort. If you enter badly, it rolls you onto your back.” The corner of her mouth shifts. “I learned the current at twenty-two. It still catches me sometimes.”

For one suspended instant, her stillness seems less like restraint than something folded very tightly.

“I miss being large enough that rooms are irrelevant,” she says. “Here, taking my proper shape requires notice to the bridge wardens, clearance from the chancellor, and an assurance that I am not making a statement about dragon sovereignty. Then the Military students gather below to critique my wings.”

Lightning opens pale caverns in the clouds. Ysolde watches them close.

“So I stand here instead.”

Her gaze drops to your ink-darkened fingertips where they emerge from your sleeves. “Knowing how to belong is not a small thing. Palaces do not provide it. Neither, apparently, do inherited pies.”

The wind eases for a breath. Somewhere behind the garden wall, a door bangs and is hastily secured.

“Did the printer know you wrote stories above her shop,” Ysolde asks, “or did she believe all that midnight pacing served some respectable purpose?”

"She knew. She once let me set a story in spare type and pinned the page beside her price list. I pretended I wasn't checking whether customers read it." I look over the storm once more. "I'm glad I came out here. Thank you." When the cold has had its fair share of us, I head back to Garvey House, with Ysolde if she's returning too. At the house I wish her goodnight and go to my room.

Ysolde considers the printer’s stratagem.

“Beside the price list ensured that people looked. She understood audiences.”

The cold claims your ears first, then works patiently through your boots. Ysolde appears untouched by it, but when you shift your weight for warmth, she turns from the parapet.

“Our shares are unequal,” she says. “Yours is full.”

She walks back with you through the wind-bent gardens. Neither of you forces conversation into the paths. At Garvey House, warmth clouds the frost along her cloak clasp, and the last servants are lowering lamps in the dining room.

You wish her goodnight.

“Goodnight, Rowan.” She pauses at the foot of the stairs. “Thank you for not asking what flying feels like. People who have not flown generally supply the answer themselves.”

In your room, a cream card has been pushed beneath the door.

**First bell — Breakfast, informal**  
**Second bell — Covenant Law: Professor Windwhisper**  
**Fourth bell — Practical Rhetoric: Professor vel Shaan**  
**Sixth bell — Conclave reception, Chancellor’s Hall**

A handwritten addition at the bottom reads: *“Informal” permits shirtsleeves. Shoes remain customary.*

Tomorrow’s fifth bell is officially empty and privately occupied.

The house settles around you in unfamiliar layers: pipes ticking behind the wall, a distant door closing, someone laughing once on the floor below. Your coat carries the storm’s mineral scent. On the desk, the framed letter still waits beside the primer, its first line visible in the lamplight.

*For my dear great-nephew, when at last he comes to Garvey House—*

I hang up my coat, wash up, and get ready for bed. I leave the framed letter where it is. I go to sleep, intending to wake in the morning with time for breakfast and the day's ordinary Academy obligations before the fifth-bell visit.

Sleep comes beneath the unfamiliar creaks of Garvey House. By morning, weak gold light lies across the framed letter, still unopened.

First-bell breakfast proves genuinely informal: Rashid wears shirtsleeves of such impeccable cut that the concession seems technical, while Aldric arrives from dawn prayer fully dressed and faintly windblown. Ysolde acknowledges you with a quiet nod over her tea.

Professor Elara Windwhisper teaches Covenant Law without notes. She is silver-haired, spare, and so economical with movement that every lifted finger arrests the oval table.

“Master Garvey’s admission restores human participation in the Conclave,” she says during a lesson on vacancies. “It does not immediately restore a Council vote. Symbolism and jurisdiction are often mistaken for one another. Your examinations will not mistake them.”

No one looks at you for more than a moment. Caelindra underlines something with unnecessary force.

At fourth bell, Professor Kira vel Shaan prowls between the same fifteen chairs, red-skinned and brisk, making the cohort identify weaknesses in arguments delivered with perfect confidence. Ashara and Rashid turn an exercise about harbor tariffs into a bloodless duel.

“Useful,” Kira concludes, “but if either of you says *self-evident* again, I’ll charge you for wasting everyone’s time.”

As you leave, her gold eyes flick to your ink-stained hand. “Garvey. Keep taking your own notes. Official summaries are written to make disagreement look tidier than it was.”

Fifth bell sounds as you descend into the common room with your courier’s misadventure in hand.

Rashid has brought a paper box of iced pastries. Seraphel presides over the tea tray. Caelindra sits where the lamplight falls best, insisting this is coincidence. Ysolde occupies the window chair, and Thessaly has brought a length of blue string, which flows between her fingers into a tiny, doomed bridge.

Ashara enters last, hair damp from washing and two knuckles freshly bandaged.

“I brought nothing,” she announces.

“You brought an injury,” Rashid says.

“Someone else’s.”

Caelindra taps your pages. “Before sixth bell, preferably. We must all become ceremonial again.”

The room settles—not silent, but attentive. Seraphel slides a cup within your reach.

“Let boots be lost and tolls accrue;  
We’re fed, and now we’re ready too.”

I take the tea and sit where everyone can hear without having to gather around me. "Three short pages. The courier has excellent reasons for everything." I read the story aloud: a courier reaches a bridge whose keeper asks a penny. He decides the stream is narrow enough to jump. He leaves his boots on the bank to keep them dry, jumps, and discovers halfway across that he has measured the distance from the wrong stone. He loses the parcel in the water. While he retrieves it, a goat carries off one boot and the current takes the other. The keeper helps him out and offers him a seat. The courier spends the walk home explaining that his mistake was taking too little of a run-up. I finish with the keeper hanging the penny toll sign a little higher, out of the goat's reach, and put my pages down. I leave the room space to react without apologizing for the story first.
